title: Triangle Angle Sum Theorem
statement: In triangle \(ABC\), the three interior angles have a total of \(180^\circ\).
summary: The three interior angles of every Euclidean triangle add to 180°.
proofIdea: Through vertex A, use the Parallel Axiom to draw line DE parallel to side BC. The Alternate Interior Angles Theorem copies the angles at B and C to angles DAB and CAE at A. Those two copied angles and angle BAC partition straight angle DAE, so Angle Addition and the Linear Pair Theorem give a total of 180°. Replacing the copies by the congruent triangle angles gives the result.
explorationPrompt: Move vertex A to make different triangles and track the three interior angle sizes. The measurements illustrate that their total remains 180°; the guided construction explains why every Euclidean triangle has that total.

proofSteps.title: Name the triangle and the target
proofSteps.detail: Let ABC be a triangle. Its three interior angles are ∠BAC, ∠ABC, and ∠BCA. The goal is to prove that their angle sizes add to 180°; the appearance of the drawing alone does not establish that total.

proofSteps.title: Draw a parallel through A
proofSteps.detail: Use the Parallel Axiom to draw the unique line through A parallel to line BC. Choose D and E on that line so D, A, and E occur in that order. Thus rays AD and AE are opposite, and ∠DAE is a straight angle.

proofSteps.title: Copy the angle at B
proofSteps.detail: Line AB cuts the parallel lines DE and BC. Angles ∠DAB and ∠ABC are alternate interior angles, so the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem gives ∠DAB ≅ ∠ABC.

proofSteps.title: Copy the angle at C
proofSteps.detail: Line AC also cuts the parallel lines DE and BC. Angles ∠CAE and ∠BCA are alternate interior angles, so the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem gives ∠CAE ≅ ∠BCA.

proofSteps.title: Partition the straight angle
proofSteps.detail: The adjacent angles ∠DAB, ∠BAC, and ∠CAE partition straight angle ∠DAE. Angle Addition and the Linear Pair Theorem therefore give ∠DAB + ∠BAC + ∠CAE = 180°.

proofSteps.title: Substitute the triangle angles
proofSteps.detail: Congruent angles have the same angle size. Replace ∠DAB by ∠ABC and ∠CAE by ∠BCA in the straight-angle sum. This gives ∠BAC + ∠ABC + ∠BCA = 180°.

corollaries.title: Corollary: Exterior Angle Theorem
corollaries.statement: In triangle ABC, extend side BC through C to D. Exterior angle ∠ACD has the same angle size as the two remote interior angles ∠BAC and ∠ABC added together.
corollaries.proof: The Triangle Angle Sum Theorem gives ∠BAC + ∠ABC + ∠BCA = 180°. Angles ∠BCA and ∠ACD form a linear pair, so ∠BCA + ∠ACD = 180°. Subtracting the common angle size ∠BCA from these equal totals gives ∠ACD = ∠BAC + ∠ABC.

corollaries.title: Corollary: Third Angle Theorem
corollaries.statement: If two pairs of corresponding angles in two triangles are congruent, then the remaining pair of corresponding angles is congruent.
corollaries.theoremLatex: \begin{gathered}\text{If }\angle BAC\cong\angle EDF\text{ and }\angle ABC\cong\angle DEF, \\ \text{then }\angle BCA\cong\angle EFD.\end{gathered}
corollaries.proof: The angle sizes in each triangle add to 180°. The two given congruent pairs have matching angle sizes, so subtracting those two matching sizes from each 180° total leaves equal sizes for ∠BCA and ∠EFD. Therefore ∠BCA ≅ ∠EFD. In particular, if each triangle has a right angle, those two right angles already supply one congruent pair. One more congruent angle pair forces the remaining pair to be congruent.

historicalContext.title: Euclid I.32 and the parallel postulate
paragraphs: Euclid's Proposition I.32 uses the same construction: draw a parallel through one triangle vertex, copy the other two angles to that vertex, and compare the three adjacent angles with a straight angle. The proposition establishes both the exterior-angle equality and the triangle's two-right-angle total.

This proof uses Euclid I.29, the direct parallel-line angle theorem, and therefore ultimately depends on the parallel postulate. Without the parallel postulate, the remaining axioms do not prove that every triangle has angle sum exactly 180°.

Other geometries behave differently: e.g. on a sphere, a triangle whose sides follow great circles has an angle sum greater than 180°, and the excess above 180° is proportional to the triangle's area. An angle sum of exactly 180° is a specifically Euclidean result.
